Conceptual framework for a “digital twin” of structures for structural monitoring and finite-element-based analysis (FEM)

Executive summary
A structural digital twin is a physics-based, data-driven virtual replica of a physical asset that continuously synchronizes monitored responses and environmental/loading data with a computational model to support diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making across the asset’s lifecycle.<cite id="6cfd565b-2">Recent structural health monitoring (SHM) strategies in civil engineering increasingly leverage digital twins, which digitally represent the structures being monitored as well as the SHM systems installed on the structures</cite><cite id="6cfd565b-3">The key features of a Digital Twin include: (1) a virtual representation of the physical asset; (2) enrichment of geometric data with semantic, engineering, and operational data from sensors; and (3) the ability to monitor and report structural behavior and health over the entire service life</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-0">BIM may be used to create digital models that can predict structural degradation using FEM and foresee consequences on integrity; an IFC-based digital twin can exchange data across platforms and update with site monitoring data, connecting to an FE model for future behavior prediction</cite>. The twin’s core computational substrate is typically an FEM, calibrated by measurements and updated over time to bridge the “model–structure” gap and enable prediction where sensors cannot reach.<cite id="60b2c612-3">All marine-structure applications reviewed require the creation of a finite element model to represent the physical structure; model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting enable diagnostics and prognostics for inspection/maintenance planning</cite><cite id="60b2c612-2">A 3D finite element model is crucial in the overall digital twin framework; updating reduced modeling error from 30% to 1% in an offshore wind turbine jacket substructure by matching measured modal properties</cite>.

1. Core definition and scope
A digital twin in civil infrastructure is a virtual representation that mirrors the physical structure’s state and behavior in near-real time, driven by a data pipeline and linked to analytical models to support integrity, safety, and serviceability management.<cite id="6cfd565b-2">Despite widespread adoption, there is no consensus definition or architecture; the review formulates a generic reference architecture and definition to serve as a blueprint for digital-twin-based SHM</cite><cite id="6cfd565b-4">Based on inflows from the physical structure, the associated FE models are updated and/or used to replicate full behavior in virtual space; practical implementation details (sensor types/locations, model development, data fusion) are case-specific</cite>. In SHM, the twin is distinguished by its lifecycle focus on monitoring, predicting, and informing decisions about health and remaining life.<cite id="6cfd565b-3">The biggest departure from traditional models is monitoring and reporting structural behavior and health throughout the service life</cite>.

2. Reference architecture and information flow
A practical architecture comprises: (i) a physical sensing and actuation layer; (ii) a digital thread linking geometry/semantics (BIM) and evolving condition state; (iii) a computational FE twin (virtual domain model); and (iv) analytics and decision services that loop back to influence operations and maintenance.<cite id="b6395cc8-0">A bridge digital twin integrates inspection automation, a semantically rich BIM updated with inspection data, and a digital twin that automatically updates with monitoring data and connects to an FE model for future behavior prediction</cite><cite id="60b2c612-3">Digital twin-based monitoring frameworks connect monitored data to FE models for diagnostics and prognostics; practical interconnection schemes exist but virtual-to-physical feedback and time-variant assessment are underexplored</cite>. The twin continuously ingests operational data (loads, deformations, strains, environmental effects) and metadata, aligns it with a common reference frame, and uses model-in-the-loop simulation to reconcile discrepancies and generate insight.<cite id="6cfd565b-3">Geometric data are enriched by semantic, engineering, and operational data extracted via sensor networks deployed on the physical asset</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-3">The essence of a bridge digital twin is to measure loads and responses and compare with FEM-based simulation automatically, affecting management decisions; reliable analysis requires updating BIM and FEM to ensure compliance with the real structure</cite>.

3. FE-centric twin design and model updating
The FE model is the twin’s virtual surrogate; its fidelity determines credibility of diagnosis and prognosis. Continuous model updating aligns the virtual and physical, enabling prediction at uninstrumented locations and estimation of remaining life.<cite id="60b2c612-0">Two finite element models are used: a ‘simulated physical model’ to generate monitored data and a digital model updated from nominal specifications using monitored responses; the setup demonstrates model updating and real-time simulation for integrity monitoring</cite><cite id="60b2c612-1">Once the FE model is updated, it predicts KPIs (e.g., stress, deformation, RUL) that feed a decision framework modifying both the structure and the twin (e.g., restricting vehicle weight or scheduling maintenance); monitoring data continuously update the numerical model, with Bayesian updating to incorporate measurement uncertainties efficiently</cite>. Evidence from marine/offshore structures shows dramatic error reduction when updating against as-installed modal properties and inspection data, underscoring the centrality of FE updating in digital-twin-driven integrity management.<cite id="60b2c612-2">Updating eigenfrequencies matched to accelerometer-measured modal properties reduced modeling error from 30% to 1%; load calibration via wave radar improved static response estimates; digital twins periodically and automatically updated with inspection data (e.g., corrosion) to reassess capacity and life extension</cite><cite id="60b2c612-3">Model updating, real-time simulation, and forecasting enable diagnostics and decision-making for inspection/maintenance planning</cite>.

4. Digital thread: from BIM/CAD to FE and sensors
A robust digital twin maintains a consistent geometry-semantic backbone (BIM/IFC) that feeds and calibrates the FE model and orchestrates sensor metadata, alignment, and visualization. This thread supports both current-state reconstruction and long-term drift (e.g., corrosion) tracking.<cite id="b6395cc8-0">Autodesk Revit has been recognized as an advanced twinning system; IFC provides interoperability; BIM/FE modeling and data integration tools form the core data layer before the digital twin</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-3">Linking BIM to the sensor system visualizes measured values, archives data, and feeds FEM-based simulation; updates to the structure are reintroduced back into BIM; BIM can automatically generate or host the FEM for comparative simulation and management decisions</cite>. Geometry updates from 3D scanning/photogrammetry can be fused with vibration-based parameter updates to maintain model accuracy over time, even when switching between beam and solid representations.<cite id="b6395cc8-4">A geometric digital twin framework generates and updates building twins from regular laser-scanner point clouds; semantic information is inferred and stored in updatable BIMs used for structural health monitoring</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-1">A framework integrates computer-vision-based 3D reconstruction with vibration measurements: accelerometer/CV data feed Bayesian model updating to refine material/stiffness properties; reconstructed meshes are aligned to beam FE models to update cross-sectional geometry and detect/quantify damage for long-term SHM</cite>.

5. Analytics stack: KPIs, forecasting, and uncertainty quantification
Digital twins compute KPIs (stresses, deformations, mode shapes, damage indices) from the updated FE model and sensor fusion, then forecast performance (e.g., cumulative damage, reliability, remaining useful life) under changing loads and boundary conditions.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Updated FE models predict KPIs and remaining useful life; a decision framework acts on both real structure and digital twin, such as restricting vehicle weights or scheduling maintenance</cite>. Predictive components include real-time or near–real-time simulation, data-driven forecasting, and probabilistic risk models; Bayesian updating endows twins with uncertainty-aware state estimation and enables virtual sensors at unmeasured locations.<cite id="60b2c612-0">Key features demonstrated include model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting using a simulated monitored data stream to drive an FE-based digital model</cite><cite id="60b2c612-1">A variational Bayesian updating scheme efficiently incorporates measurement uncertainties and enables prediction at inaccessible or fatigue-prone locations</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-2">Digital twins are physics-based probabilistic simulation models continuously updated with sensor information and load history; frameworks have been demonstrated on laboratory trusses and real-time SHM for vibration-based updating, with application to cathedrals for damage prediction</cite>. The analytics layer must also provide data mining and quality assurance for long-term operation and standardization of monitoring systems.<cite id="60b2c612-3">To fully exploit digital twins, standardization, redundancy, and data quality assurance are needed; a dedicated data mining capability should be incorporated due to the vast amounts of data generated</cite>.

6. Closed-loop decision framework
A digital twin is effective only when it closes the loop: operational decisions (loads, inspections, maintenance) trigger changes in the physical asset and propagate updates back to the digital twin, creating a feedback cycle that improves fidelity and future predictions.<cite id="60b2c612-1">A closed cycle runs from real structure to simulation (model updating) and from simulation to real structure via a decision framework (e.g., restricting vehicle weight, performing maintenance/repair)</cite>. This closed-loop underpins integrity management, inspection planning, and life extension strategies informed by updated FE models and reliability/RUL estimates.<cite id="60b2c612-2">Engineering reassessment for corrosion and fatigue is performed on periodically updated FE models to support life extension</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-3">Automatic comparison of measured loads/responses with FEM-based simulation affects management decisions; updates to the existing structure are reintroduced into BIM to maintain compliance</cite>.

7. Data management, synchronization, and interoperability
Operationalization hinges on a data management system that supports real-time access, preprocessing, synchronization across sensor streams, and a common metadata schema, typically anchored in BIM/IFC for lifecycle semantics.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Implementing a digital twin poses challenges in data management: real-time access and preprocessing are required to avoid transferring/storing large volumes; when combining datasets from different systems, synchronization and a defined metadata schema are critical</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-0">IFC provides an interoperability platform to exchange data across non-native formats; BIM/FE modeling and data integration tools are core to the digital twin pipeline</cite>. In practice, the twin orchestrates point-cloud-to-BIM pipelines, sensor data alignment to the BIM reference, and FE model parameterization, enabling change detection and model adaptation.<cite id="b6395cc8-4">Point-cloud processing extracts position and section shape; function and section family are inferred to automatically generate or update BIM as the twin’s virtual model for SHM</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-2">BIM provides a geometric reference frame for UAV imagery; overlaying BIM on photographs organizes and classifies structural components; BIM plus visual survey and analytical model yields predictive digital twins</cite>.

8. Implementation pathways and governance
- Bridge and building asset managers can start from BIM/IFC, instrument critical locations, and link to FE models for as-built/ageing-aware reassessment; 3D scanning/photogrammetry and computer vision feed geometry updates, while vibration and strain sensors provide parameter updates.<cite id="b6395cc8-0">BIM/IFC-based smart bridge management uses FEM to predict degradation and its impact on integrity; BIM can be the basis for FE models that update with monitoring data for future behavior prediction</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-1">CV-based 3D reconstruction and vibration measurements can jointly update beam FE models’ material and geometric properties, enabling damage detection and quantification</cite>. 
- Offshore/wind and marine structures benefit from eigenfrequency-based updating and environmental load calibration, with twins informing maintenance and life extension under corrosion/fatigue processes.<cite id="60b2c612-2">Updating to match measured modal properties reduced modeling error from 30% to 1%; wave load calibration improved static response; twins updated periodically with inspection data for corrosion/fatigue reassessment and life extension</cite>. 
- Cultural/historic buildings and cathedrals can use calibrated FE twins for risk assessment and lifetime damage evolution modeling, demonstrated probabilistically on laboratory and full-scale structures.<cite id="b6395cc8-2">Probabilistic digital twin frameworks for risk assessment and decision-making have been demonstrated on laboratory truss structures and real-time SHM; a calibrated digital twin predicted existing damage in a Milan cathedral and modeled lifetime evolution</cite>.

Governance entails defining data standards, redundancy and QA for long-term deployment, change management from BIM to FE and back, and secure access control across lifecycle phases.<cite id="60b2c612-3">Challenges include standardization, enhanced redundancy for long-term applications, and monitored data quality assurance; dedicated data mining capability is needed</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-3">Modifications resulting from twin analysis are introduced back into BIM; linking BIM to sensors and FEM-based simulation requires robust processes and interfaces</cite>.

9. Practical considerations and trade-offs
Digital twins deliver predictive insight and virtual instrumentation but are highly asset- and case-specific; success depends on sensor strategy, FE abstraction level, and data fusion algorithms tailored to objectives.<cite id="6cfd565b-4">Field implementation faces challenges because sensor types/locations, structural model development, and data fusion algorithms depend strongly on case-specific objectives</cite>. Computational cost of real-time FE and continuous updating can be high; uncertainty-aware Bayesian schemes and selective virtual sensing mitigate risk while preserving timeliness.<cite id="60b2c612-1">A variational Bayesian updating approach significantly reduces computational effort compared to traditional sampling-based schemes while incorporating measurement uncertainties</cite>. Integration complexity arises from aligning new geometry with simplified FE models; systematic update procedures and semantic alignment (BIM/IFC) are key to maintaining consistency.<cite id="b6395cc8-1">Updating digital twin models systematically in a manner consistent with engineering assumptions (e.g., beam vs. solid) is key; a proposed framework aligns reconstructed meshes to beam models and updates cross-sectional properties</cite>.

10. A step-by-step blueprint (Marco conceptual)
- Define scope and digital thread: Capture the asset lifecycle, select BIM/IFC standard, and designate BIM as the semantic backbone that will feed and calibrate the FE twin and orchestrate sensors and KPIs.<cite id="b6395cc8-0">BIM/IFC provides interoperability and a path to automatically update with monitoring data and connect to FE models for prediction</cite>. 
- Instrument and pipeline data: Deploy sensors (vibration, strain, deformation, environmental), define metadata schema, and implement preprocessing, synchronization, and real-time access layers; align imagery/point clouds to BIM for geometry/semantic updates.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Real-time access and preprocessing are required; synchronization and metadata schema are critical when combining datasets from different systems</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-4">Laser-scanner point clouds are processed to infer geometry and semantics and automatically update BIM as the virtual twin model for SHM</cite>. 
- Build and validate the FE twin: Create an FE model from BIM/CAD; establish “simulated physical model” for calibration if necessary; perform initial offline validation (modal testing, load tests) and then online updating with measured responses to close the model–structure gap.<cite id="60b2c612-0">A simulated physical model can generate monitored data; the digital model is developed from nominal specifications and updated using monitored responses to demonstrate model updating and real-time simulation</cite><cite id="60b2c612-2">Updating to match measured modal properties can reduce modeling error from 30% to 1%, and load calibration improves accuracy</cite>. 
- Implement analytics: Define KPIs and forecasting models; deploy Bayesian model updating to integrate sensor uncertainty; enable virtual sensors to report at unmeasured locations; embed probabilistic risk and RUL modules for maintenance/inspection planning.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Bayesian updating enriches measurements with simulation to provide reliability and RUL predictions and insert virtual sensors at inaccessible positions, feeding a decision framework</cite><cite id="60b2c612-3">Model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting support diagnostics and decision-making for inspection/maintenance</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-2">Digital twins are physics-based probabilistic models continuously updated with sensor/load data to inform risk assessment and decisions</cite>. 
- Close the loop: Integrate decisions (load limits, inspection schedules, repairs) into the twin; update BIM/FE models with inspection outcomes and degradation data; automate re-meshing/parameterization updates where needed to reflect structural changes over time.<cite id="60b2c612-1">A decision framework changes both the real structure and the digital twin, such as reducing vehicle weight or performing maintenance/repair</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-3">Updates from structural modifications are reintroduced into BIM; the digital twin compares measured and simulated behavior to affect management decisions</cite>. 
- Govern and scale: Adopt lifecycle data standards, QA/QC protocols, redundancy for long-term deployments, and data mining capabilities; plan for periodic recalibration and life-extension reassessments using updated FE twins.<cite id="60b2c612-3">Standardization, enhanced redundancy, and data quality assurance are needed; a dedicated data mining capability should be incorporated</cite><cite id="60b2c612-2">Periodic, automatic updating with inspection data supports engineering reassessment concerning corrosion and fatigue for life extension</cite>.

Illustrative case study patterns
- Laboratory and small-scale demonstrators show how twins can infer hidden stresses and remaining life, even when direct access is limited, by fusing simulated/observed data and updating FE models for forecasting.<cite id="60b2c612-0">A cantilever plate case demonstrates model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting to monitor a fatigue-prone area and assess remaining life despite limited sensor access</cite>. 
- Real-world bridges and buildings implement BIM-to-twin pipelines where point clouds and sensors update geometry and parameters, while FEM-based comparisons drive inspection and maintenance strategies.<cite id="b6395cc8-3">BIM linked to sensors feeds FEM-based simulation for automatic comparison and decision-making; updates are reintroduced into BIM</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-4">Automatic generation and updating of gDTs from laser scans supports structural monitoring services via updatable BIMs</cite>. 
- Historic structures demonstrate probabilistic twins calibrated against vibration and visual surveys, achieving damage detection and lifetime evolution prediction.<cite id="b6395cc8-2">A calibrated digital twin predicted existing damage in a historic Milan cathedral and modeled lifetime evolution</cite>.

Takeaways for a “Marco” conceptual gemelo digital (structural monitoring + FEM)
- Start from a clear definition and reference architecture: virtual asset + sensing + FE model + analytics + decisions, with BIM/IFC as the digital backbone.<cite id="6cfd565b-2">A multivocal review derives a generic reference architecture and definitions for digital twins in civil engineering to blueprint SHM applications</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-0">BIM/IFC-based twins integrate inspection data, update with monitoring, and connect to FE models for prediction</cite>. 
- Make the FE model first-class: treat it as a living asset proxy; design updating strategies (modal, damage, load, geometry) to minimize modeling error and unlock virtual instrumentation.<cite id="60b2c612-2">Updating reduced modeling error from 30% to 1% by matching measured modal properties and calibrating loads</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-1">CV geometry and vibration data jointly update beam FE models to detect/quantify damage for SHM</cite>. 
- Build a robust digital thread: automate BIM↔FE↔sensor synchronization, embed uncertainty, and support real-time operations with preprocessing and metadata standards.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Real-time access, preprocessing, synchronization, and metadata schema are essential for multi-sensor integration in digital twins</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-4">Automatic BIM generation/update from point clouds provides the virtual model for gDT-based SHM</cite>. 
- Realize value via closed-loop governance: decisions must propagate back to update the digital thread, improving twin fidelity and informing future interventions; plan for lifecycle QA, standardization, and data mining.<cite id="60b2c612-1">A closed cycle links model updating to decision frameworks that change both the structure and the twin</cite><cite id="60b2c612-3">Standardization, redundancy, data quality assurance, and data mining are needed to exploit digital twin potential</cite>.

Limitations and tailoring
Evidence shows strong benefits but also that implementation details are case-specific; sensor placement, FE abstraction, and data fusion must be tuned to asset type and risk profile.<cite id="6cfd565b-4">Field implementation challenges include sensor types/locations, model development, and data fusion algorithms that depend strongly on case-specific objectives</cite>. Computational demands can be alleviated by event-driven updates, Bayesian efficiency, and selective virtual sensing, while long-term reliability hinges on data governance and periodic recalibration.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Variational Bayesian updating reduces computational burden while incorporating uncertainties and enabling virtual sensors</cite><cite id="60b2c612-2">Periodic updating with inspection data maintains twin fidelity for life-extension assessments</cite>.

Appendix: Key definitions to anchor discussions
- Digital twin (civil SHM): A physics-based probabilistic simulation model of a physical structure, continuously updated with sensor information and load history to monitor behavior and predict performance over the service life.<cite id="b6395cc8-2">Digital twins are physics-based probabilistic models continuously updated using sensor data and load history from the physical system</cite><cite id="6cfd565b-3">The twin monitors and reports structural behavior and health throughout the service life, enriching geometry with semantic and operational data from sensors</cite>. 
- FEM-in-the-loop: The FE model is not merely a design artifact; it actively ingests monitored data for updating, issues KPIs and forecasts, and informs maintenance and load management in a closed loop with the physical asset.<cite id="60b2c612-1">Updated FE models provide KPIs (stress, deformation, RUL) and feed a decision framework; monitoring data continuously update the numerical model</cite><cite id="60b2c612-3">Model updating, real-time simulation, and forecasting enable structural diagnostics and decision-making</cite>. 
- Digital thread: The persistent, semantically rich link from design (BIM/CAD) through construction and operations to the operational FE twin, ensuring geometry, material, and condition states are consistent and updatable across systems.<cite id="b6395cc8-0">IFC-based interoperability allows data exchange across non-native formats; BIM can be the basis for FE models that update with monitoring data and connect to FE for future behavior prediction</cite><cite id="b6395cc8-3">BIM linked to sensors and FEM-based simulation supports automatic comparison and management decisions, with updates reintroduced into BIM</cite>.

Title: A multivocal literature review of digital twins, architectures, and elements in civil engineering
Snippet: Recent structural health monitoring (SHM) strategies in civil engineering increasingly leverage digital twins, which digitally represent the structures being monitored as well as the SHM systems installed on the structures. Despite the widespread adoption of digital twin applications in recent years in SHM, there is a lack of agreement on a common definition of digital twins. Furthermore, there is no consensus on digital twin architectures and on the internal elements that constitute digital twins. A common digital twin definition would advance digital twin implementations and operability, and insights into digital twin architectures and digital twin elements would be vital to enhance the reliability and performance of digital-twin-based SHM systems. A significant number of digital twin definitions have been proposed and a plethora of reviews have been published; however, little emphasis has been given to digital twin architectures and internal elements. This paper presents a multivocal review of digital twins in civil engineering, aiming to provide a panorama of the digital twin landscape in civil engineering with explicit insights into the architectures and internal elements used in digital twin applications. From a methodological standpoint, the review follows a twofold approach that encompasses (i) peer-reviewed, indexed literature (“white literature”) as well as (ii) non-indexed sources (“gray literature”) that include industrial digital twin applications. Besides the multivocal review, a generic digital twin reference architecture is drawn from the review results and a digital twin definition is formulated both in an informal and formal (i.e., mathematical) manner. It is expected that the generic reference architecture and the definitions proposed in this study may serve as a blueprint for digital-twin-based SHM applications, with significant implications for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers in structural health monitoring.
</snippet>

Title: Digital twin enabled structural integrity management: Critical review and framework development
Snippet: An illustrative example is presented to demonstrate the key features of the proposed digital twin framework, namely model updating, real-time simulation, and datadriven forecasting. A cantilever plate with a central cutout subjected to a wave force at its free edge is considered (Figure 3). The central cut-out leads to a stress concentration in an area closed to the cut-out corner, which is therefore regarded as a fatigue-prone area with high criticality in relation to structural integrity. The objective is to monitor this fatigue-prone area and ultimately assess its remaining life to support decision making with respect to inspection planning or other interventions. However, monitoring cannot be conducted proximal to this hotspot and thus measurements taken from other locations are required. Although this numerical example may appear to be trivial, it is sufficiently representative of a real-world scenario where the accessibility to a damage-prone critical location is limited. Thus, physical monitoring can only be performed at locations with better accessibility that are likely to be less structurally prominent. For now, it can help demonstrate the key features of the developed digital twin framework in a tractable manner. The monitored response will be obtained via a dynamic finite element analysis performed using a 'simulated physical model'. After completing the finite element simulation, the time histories of the responses at eight locations will be acquired (see Figure 4). These data represent the measurements from physical strain gauges. Strictly speaking they should be denoted as 'simulated monitored data'. However, to avoid confusion, the term 'monitored data' will be used hereafter. 

For the present illustrative example, two finite element models will be developed, a 'simulated physical model' which provides the monitored data and a digital model which shall be used in conjunction with the monitored data. Both model is developed using four-node shell elements with the same mesh density (25 mm 3 25 mm). The 'simulated physical model' is developed based on the actual geometric dimension, material property and boundary condition specified in Table 2, while the digital model is developed based on the nominal specification. 

For illustrative purposes, the actual and nominal specifications only differ in plate thickness, elastic modulus, and rotational stiffness around the y-axis.
</snippet>

Title: Bayesian model calibration and damage detection for a digital twin of a bridge demonstrator

Title: Digital twin enabled structural integrity management: Critical review and framework development
Snippet: This paper presents a critical review of literature on the emerging technology known as digital twin and its application in structural integrity management for marine structures. The review defines digital twin in relation to structural integrity management as a virtual representation of a physical structure that mirrors the same structural conditions in real time. Twinning is a dynamic process that involves reducing the discrepancy between the virtual representation and physical structure, which is achieved with the aid of monitored data. Regarding the state-of-the-art concerning marine structure applications, all require the creation of a finite element model to represent the physical structure. Several practical schemes for physical to virtual interconnection have been proposed, but few researchers have concentrated on virtual to physical feedback. In addition, most works have focused only on assessing the current states of structures. To address this, a digital twin-based monitoring framework is proposed and three key enabling technologies, namely model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting are demonstrated using a numerical case study. Such technologies enable structural diagnostics, as well as prognostics, to support decision making such as inspection/maintenance planning. Based on the case study, the opportunities and associated challenges of digital twin are discussed. For instance, to fully exploit the potential of digital twin, challenges related to monitoring systems such as standardisation, enhanced redundancy for long-term application, and monitored data quality assurance need to be addressed. Further, because digital twin can avail a vast amount of data, a dedicated data mining capability should also be incorporated.
</snippet>

At the same time, it also provides the information required in the subsequent stages of the construction process. In the operational phase, by linking it to the sensor system, it serves as an interface of the digital twin, allowing visualization of the measured values and providing access to archival data. Modifications to the existing structure resulting from the twin analysis are also introduced back into the BIM model. In the design and operational stages, the usefulness of the BIM model can be extended to generate a finite element analysis (FEM) model which, in addition to the BIM counterpart, plays an equally crucial role in the whole system. The essence of the digital twin is to measure the loads and responses of the structure and then compare the results with the computational FEM-based simulation. The comparison is performed automatically and affects decisions and strategies in the management process. However, it is not possible to perform a reliable analysis without updating the BIM and FEM models to ensure their compliance with the real structure.

Title: Automatic generation of structural geometric digital twins from point clouds
Snippet: A geometric digital twin (gDT) model capable of leveraging acquired 3D geometric data plays a vital role in digitizing the process of structural health monitoring. This study presents a framework for generating and updating digital twins of existing buildings by inferring semantic information from as-is point clouds (gDT’s data) acquired regularly from laser scanners (gDT’s connection). The information is stored in updatable Building Information Models (BIMs) as gDT’s virtual model, and dimensional outputs are extracted for structural health monitoring (gDT’s service) of different structural members and shapes (gDT’s physical part). First, geometric information, including position and section shape, is obtained from the acquired point cloud using domain-specific contextual knowledge and supervised classification. Then, structural members’ function and section family type is inferred from geometric information. Finally, a BIM is automatically generated or updated as the virtual model of an existing facility and incorporated within the gDT for structural health monitoring. Experiments on real-world construction data are performed to illustrate the efficiency and precision of the proposed model for creating as-is gDT of building structural members.

Title: A multivocal literature review of digital twins, architectures, and elements in civil engineering
Snippet: Recent structural health monitoring (SHM) strategies in civil engineering increasingly leverage digital twins, which digitally represent the structures being monitored as well as the SHM systems installed on the structures. Despite the widespread adoption of digital twin applications in recent years in SHM, there is a lack of agreement on a common definition of digital twins. Furthermore, there is no consensus on digital twin architectures and on the internal elements that constitute digital twins. A common digital twin definition would advance digital twin implementations and operability, and insights into digital twin architectures and digital twin elements would be vital to enhance the reliability and performance of digital-twin-based SHM systems. A significant number of digital twin definitions have been proposed and a plethora of reviews have been published; however, little emphasis has been given to digital twin architectures and internal elements. This paper presents a multivocal review of digital twins in civil engineering, aiming to provide a panorama of the digital twin landscape in civil engineering with explicit insights into the architectures and internal elements used in digital twin applications. From a methodological standpoint, the review follows a twofold approach that encompasses (i) peer-reviewed, indexed literature (“white literature”) as well as (ii) non-indexed sources (“gray literature”) that include industrial digital twin applications. Besides the multivocal review, a generic digital twin reference architecture is drawn from the review results and a digital twin definition is formulated both in an informal and formal (i.e., mathematical) manner. It is expected that the generic reference architecture and the definitions proposed in this study may serve as a blueprint for digital-twin-based SHM applications, with significant implications for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers in structural health monitoring.

Title: Digital twin enabled structural integrity management: Critical review and framework development
Snippet: An illustrative example is presented to demonstrate the key features of the proposed digital twin framework, namely model updating, real-time simulation, and datadriven forecasting. A cantilever plate with a central cutout subjected to a wave force at its free edge is considered (Figure 3). The central cut-out leads to a stress concentration in an area closed to the cut-out corner, which is therefore regarded as a fatigue-prone area with high criticality in relation to structural integrity. The objective is to monitor this fatigue-prone area and ultimately assess its remaining life to support decision making with respect to inspection planning or other interventions. However, monitoring cannot be conducted proximal to this hotspot and thus measurements taken from other locations are required. Although this numerical example may appear to be trivial, it is sufficiently representative of a real-world scenario where the accessibility to a damage-prone critical location is limited. Thus, physical monitoring can only be performed at locations with better accessibility that are likely to be less structurally prominent. For now, it can help demonstrate the key features of the developed digital twin framework in a tractable manner. The monitored response will be obtained via a dynamic finite element analysis performed using a 'simulated physical model'. After completing the finite element simulation, the time histories of the responses at eight locations will be acquired (see Figure 4). These data represent the measurements from physical strain gauges. Strictly speaking they should be denoted as 'simulated monitored data'. However, to avoid confusion, the term 'monitored data' will be used hereafter. 

For the present illustrative example, two finite element models will be developed, a 'simulated physical model' which provides the monitored data and a digital model which shall be used in conjunction with the monitored data. Both model is developed using four-node shell elements with the same mesh density (25 mm 3 25 mm). The 'simulated physical model' is developed based on the actual geometric dimension, material property and boundary condition specified in Table 2, while the digital model is developed based on the nominal specification. 

For illustrative purposes, the actual and nominal specifications only differ in plate thickness, elastic modulus, and rotational stiffness around the y-axis.

Title: Bayesian model calibration and damage detection for a digital twin of a bridge demonstrator
Snippet: Once the finite element model is updated, it can be used for predicting (5) key performance indicators KPI, for example, the stress at a relevant position, a deformation that has not been measured, or even a prediction of the remaining useful life.Based on the KPIs, a decision framework (6) is then installed which changes both the real structure (7) and the digital twin (8), for example, by reducing the maximum vehicle weight, or performing maintenance or repair.As such, this digital twin concept characterizes a closed cycle from the real structure to the simulation model (via model updating) and from the simulation model to the real structure via the decision framework.

The main advantage of the concept is that the measurement data is enriched with the simulation models to provide additional information such as the prediction of the reliability and the remaining useful life, inserting virtual sensors by extracting information from the numerical model at positions that are not directly measured (e.g., inaccessible or not directly measurable such as fatigue damage), identifying gradual changes (e.g., damage, creep) or using the numerical model to investigate different maintenance procedures.

In this approach, monitoring data is used to continuously update the numerical model.Furthermore, the incorporation of measurement uncertainties in the model updating using a Bayesian model updating procedure is demonstrated, with a specific variational approach that is computationally efficient and thus requires significantly less computational effort compared to traditional sampling based schemes.The implementation of such a digital twin poses many challenges and the goal of this work is to share the authors experiences when working on a lab-demonstrator bridge.The experimental data and the code are published as complementary material to encourage others to test their methods.

The first of those challenges is the necessity of an appropriate data management system.Based on the requirement (e.g., real-time access to the data, preprocessing of data to avoid transferring and storing large amounts of data), different options are possible.In particular when combining data sets acquired from different measurement systems, as demonstrated in this work, challenges related to the synchronization and a definition of metadata schema to correctly identify the different setups arise.

Title: Digital twin enabled structural integrity management: Critical review and framework development
Snippet: As inferred from the SSC project scope and the foregoing reviewed literature, the numerical twin of a structure, usually in the form of a 3D finite element model, plays a crucial role in the overall digital twin framework in terms of virtual domain modelling. 5,37 The accuracy of this numerical model in terms of representing the physical assets will dictate the credibility of any diagnostics and prognostics made with respect to structural integrity. Whilst finite element modelling has been widely applied in marine structures, there is inevitably a discrepancy between the design specification and actual configuration, such as wall thickness of tubular structures. In view of finite element model updating, Augustyn et al. 40 developed an updating scheme by finding the best match between the eigenfrequencies predicted by finite element model and the as-installed modal properties measured by accelerometers. The application of the proposed scheme to the jacket substructure of an offshore wind turbine showed an error reduction from 30% to 1%. To further reduce the uncertainty in modelling, a calibration of the wave loads was implemented by the same author using wave radar so that the static response to wave load could be accurately estimated. 41 These techniques were incorporated into the digital twin framework for offshore wind structures, as discussed in Refs. 51,52 n addition to the improvement of numerical modelling, it is equally important to account for the timevariant degradation of physical assets, such as corrosion wastage. Therefore, the finite element model developed during the initial design of the structure must be updated periodically. In this respect, Boutrot et al. 42 discussed a methodology based on 3D digital twin for the engineering reassessment of ageing offshore units from the viewpoint of life extension. The digital twin, in the form of a 3D finite element model, was periodically and automatically updated with critical inspection data on corrosion wastage. Engineering reassessment concerning corrosion and fatigue was performed on the updated model using a rule-based environment load calculation.

Title: Digital twin enabled structural integrity management: Critical review and framework development
Snippet: This paper presents a critical review of literature on the emerging technology known as digital twin and its application in structural integrity management for marine structures. The review defines digital twin in relation to structural integrity management as a virtual representation of a physical structure that mirrors the same structural conditions in real time. Twinning is a dynamic process that involves reducing the discrepancy between the virtual representation and physical structure, which is achieved with the aid of monitored data. Regarding the state-of-the-art concerning marine structure applications, all require the creation of a finite element model to represent the physical structure. Several practical schemes for physical to virtual interconnection have been proposed, but few researchers have concentrated on virtual to physical feedback. In addition, most works have focused only on assessing the current states of structures. To address this, a digital twin-based monitoring framework is proposed and three key enabling technologies, namely model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting are demonstrated using a numerical case study. Such technologies enable structural diagnostics, as well as prognostics, to support decision making such as inspection/maintenance planning. Based on the case study, the opportunities and associated challenges of digital twin are discussed. For instance, to fully exploit the potential of digital twin, challenges related to monitoring systems such as standardisation, enhanced redundancy for long-term application, and monitored data quality assurance need to be addressed. Further, because digital twin can avail a vast amount of data, a dedicated data mining capability should also be incorporated.

snippet.text: This paper presents a critical review of literature on the emerging technology known as digital twin and its application in structural integrity management for marine structures. The review defines digital twin in relation to structural integrity management as a virtual representation of a physical structure that mirrors the same structural conditions in real time. Twinning is a dynamic process that involves reducing the discrepancy between the virtual representation and physical structure, which is achieved with the aid of monitored data. Regarding the state-of-the-art concerning marine structure applications, all require the creation of a finite element model to represent the physical structure. Several practical schemes for physical to virtual interconnection have been proposed, but few researchers have concentrated on virtual to physical feedback. In addition, most works have focused only on assessing the current states of structures. To address this, a digital twin-based monitoring framework is proposed and three key enabling technologies, namely model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting are demonstrated using a numerical case study. Such technologies enable structural diagnostics, as well as prognostics, to support decision making such as inspection/maintenance planning. Based on the case study, the opportunities and associated challenges of digital twin are discussed. For instance, to fully exploit the potential of digital twin, challenges related to monitoring systems such as standardisation, enhanced redundancy for long-term application, and monitored data quality assurance need to be addressed. Further, because digital twin can avail a vast amount of data, a dedicated data mining capability should also be incorporated.

snippet.text: Digital Twin is an effective platform for analyzing, visualizing, and interpreting the condition of as-built structures based on sensor measurement data. Based on the data inflow from the as-built structures, the associated models (typically finite element models) are updated, and/or the full behaviors of the structures are replicated in the virtual space. Despite its potential, field implementation of digital twin concepts often faces challenge, because the specific forms of digital twin, such as sensor types/locations, structural model development, and data fusion algorithms, depend strongly on the case-specific objectives. Focusing on the digital twin concepts assisted by computer vision techniques, this research aims at facilitating the implementation of those concepts by presenting the definition, setting, and preliminary results of digital twin in different application contexts, including post-earthquake building assessment and structural health monitoring based on multiple types of measurements. This research is expected to contribute to the broader impact of digital twin concepts in the structural engineering community.

A cantilever plate with a central cutout subjected to a wave force at its free edge is considered (Figure 3). However, monitoring cannot be conducted proximal to this hotspot and thus measurements taken from other locations are required. Although this numerical example may appear to be trivial, it is sufficiently representative of a real-world scenario where the accessibility to a damage-prone critical location is limited. Snippet: Building information modeling (BIM) may be used to create digital models that can then be utilized to predict structural degradation using nite element methods (FEM) and foresee the consequences of such decay on the integrity of structures [79,80,89]. In a smart BMS, the precise modeling of the current state and forecasting of future behavior are crucial components [73]. Autodesk Revit, the most widely used commercial BIM software, has been recognized as one of the most sophisticated digital twinning systems by several writers in this study [73]. In addition, an industry foundation class (IFC) platform is provided, allowing data to be exchanged across nonnative le formats [90]. A neutral le format for transmitting digital building models, such as IFC, can help alleviate interoperability di culties [74]. 

To design a BMS, several stages must be considered. e signi cance of conducting routine bridge inspections was rst recognized. e critical concerns with present techniques and technology were improving inspection and damage detection. e second component, digital models, focused on BIM, FE modeling, and data integration tools across platforms. Finally, the third segment addressed digital twins, revealing a lack of clarity on the de nition of the Digital Twin for the construction sector and the fact that, while expanding, the approach to bridge management is still in its infancy. Title: Digital Twin of Built Structures assisted by Computer Vision Techniques: Overview and Preliminary Results
Snippet: Computer vision techniques, together with image surveys, can reconstruct 3D shapes of the photographed objects, providing geometric information relevant to the structural conditions. Some researchers have investigated approaches for converting the reconstructed shapes into structural mesh models directly, e.g., (Zhang & Lin, 2021). While such purely data driven approaches demonstrate promising results, their integration into existing digital twin frameworks is not necessarily straightforward. One of the reasons is that FE models used by typical digital twin applications put modeling assumptions and simplifications, e.g., using beam models, not 3D solid models that replicate the target structural geometry exactly. Those modeling assumptions are the consequence of engineering decisions related to the purpose of the model and the expected levels of detail. An approach to updating digital twin models systematically in a manner consistent with those modeling assumptions is a key to integrating 3D geometric measurement into existing digital twin frameworks. 

A framework for incorporating computer vision-based 3D reconstruction and geometry measurement into digital twin models for structural dynamics applications has been proposed by the author's group, which is shown in Figure 2 ( Lai et al., 2022). Starting from a simplified initial FE model (beam elements are considered therein), the framework performs a sequence of vibration measurement and image surveys to update model material and geometric properties, respectively. The vibration-based model updating is performed by the measurement by accelerometers and/or computer vision techniques, followed by the application of Bayesian model updating techniques, e.g., (Yuen et al., 2006). The geometry update is performed in the following steps: (1) image survey and 3D reconstruction by Structure from Motion (SfM) method, (2) alignment of digital twin model to the reconstructed mesh Figure 2 Framework for digital twin model updating based on vibration measurement and computer vision-based 3D reconstruction (Lai et al., 2022). 

model, (3) slicing the reconstructed mesh model along the aligned beam elements of the digital twin model, (4) evaluating and updating cross-sectional geometric properties, such as areas and second moments of area. Title: Post-Earthquake Building Evaluation Using UAVs: A BIM-Based Digital Twin Framework
Snippet: Such approaches typically generate a 3D reconstruction from site photographs aligned in the BIM geometric reference frame. Once aligned, semantic information stored in the BIM is used to track construction progress. For example, the user can assess, on an element-wise basis, whether construction is on schedule and whether the as-built geometry conforms to the design. BIM can fill a similar role for post-earthquake inspection, providing a way to store data, establish a geometric reference frame for UAV imagery, and efficiently organize and classify structural components by overlaying BIM on photographs. Using BIM requires either a modern target building, where a BIM is created as part of the design process, or sufficient stakeholder investment to justify creating a BIM to aid in post-earthquake inspection. On its own, however, BIM is not predictive; to predict global damage and future performance, the BIM and visual survey must be combined with an analytical model of the building. 

Digital twins have been proposed as a means to provide predictive information about an as-built structure. As used herein, a digital twin is a physics-based probabilistic simulation model that is continuously updated using sensor information and load history from the physical system [30]. Such systems have been proposed and deployed for manufacturing, industrial, aerospace, and civil engineering applications [31,32]. In civil structural health monitoring, frameworks have been proposed that meet the criteria of a digital twin. For example, Hughes et al. [33] described a probabilistic system for risk assessment and decision making using sensor data and demonstrate its application on a laboratory truss structure. Zhu et al. [34] developed a real-time digital twin framework for structural health monitoring applications using vibration data, whereby the digital model can be continuously and efficiently updated to reflect changes to the structure. Gardner et al. [35] proposed a scheme to characterize and predict unanticipated nonlinear acceleration responses with a digital twin. However, while useful for updating a digital twin for predicting seismic response, many of these examples have been limited to simulation or scaled laboratory experiments. Angjeliu et al. [36] developed a digital twin model of a historic cathedral in Milan, Italy, and successfully predict existing damage using their calibrated digital twin to model the evolution of the structure through its lifetime.

Title: The Concept of Creating Digital Twins of Bridges Using Load Tests
Snippet: In the construction industry, it can be achieved using structural health monitoring [23,24] aided by novel sensing and digitization techniques such as laser scanning or photogrammetry [25,26], Internet of Things (IoT) [27], machine learning, and artificial intelligence [28], as well as virtual reality (VR), mixed reality (MR), or augmented reality (AR) [29]. Digital twins based on these elements were successfully developed and tested as components of tools for asset management systems [30,31], damage detection [32][33][34][35], and performance optimization [36]. 

Usually, a digital twin of a building is an enhanced version of a model following the Building Information Modeling (BIM) paradigm [37]. The BIM model, as a basis for the digital twin, can be supplemented with auxiliary techniques and tools to form a faithful reproduction of the building, sensitive to its ongoing changes (Figure 1). The BIM model can be created and developed at the design stage, e.g., to generate drawings, quantity take-offs, or schedules. At the same time, it also provides the information required in the subsequent stages of the construction process. In the operational phase, by linking it to the sensor system, it serves as an interface of the digital twin, allowing visualization of the measured values and providing access to archival data. Modifications to the existing structure resulting from the twin analysis are also introduced back into the BIM model. In the design and operational stages, the usefulness of the BIM model can be extended to generate a finite element analysis (FEM) model which, in addition to the BIM counterpart, plays an equally crucial role in the whole system. The essence of the digital twin is to measure the loads and responses of the structure and then compare the results with the computational FEM-based simulation. The comparison is performed automatically and affects decisions and strategies in the management process. However, it is not possible to perform a reliable analysis without updating the BIM and FEM models to ensure their compliance with the real structure.

Title: Automatic generation of structural geometric digital twins from point clouds
Snippet: A geometric digital twin (gDT) model capable of leveraging acquired 3D geometric data plays a vital role in digitizing the process of structural health monitoring. This study presents a framework for generating and updating digital twins of existing buildings by inferring semantic information from as-is point clouds (gDT’s data) acquired regularly from laser scanners (gDT’s connection). The information is stored in updatable Building Information Models (BIMs) as gDT’s virtual model, and dimensional outputs are extracted for structural health monitoring (gDT’s service) of different structural members and shapes (gDT’s physical part). First, geometric information, including position and section shape, is obtained from the acquired point cloud using domain-specific contextual knowledge and supervised classification. Then, structural members’ function and section family type is inferred from geometric information. Finally, a BIM is automatically generated or updated as the virtual model of an existing facility and incorporated within the gDT for structural health monitoring. Experiments on real-world construction data are performed to illustrate the efficiency and precision of the proposed model for creating as-is gDT of building structural members.

Modifications to the existing structure resulting from the twin analysis are also introduced back into the BIM model. snippet.text: A geometric digital twin (gDT) model capable of leveraging acquired 3D geometric data plays a vital role in digitizing the process of structural health monitoring. This study presents a framework for generating and updating digital twins of existing buildings by inferring semantic information from as-is point clouds (gDT’s data) acquired regularly from laser scanners (gDT’s connection). The information is stored in updatable Building Information Models (BIMs) as gDT’s virtual model, and dimensional outputs are extracted for structural health monitoring (gDT’s service) of different structural members and shapes (gDT’s physical part). First, geometric information, including position and section shape, is obtained from the acquired point cloud using domain-specific contextual knowledge and supervised classification. Then, structural members’ function and section family type is inferred from geometric information. Finally, a BIM is automatically generated or updated as the virtual model of an existing facility and incorporated within the gDT for structural health monitoring. Experiments on real-world construction data are performed to illustrate the efficiency and precision of the proposed model for creating as-is gDT of building structural members.

documents.title: Digital Twin of Built Structures assisted by Computer Vision Techniques: Overview and Preliminary Results
documents.snippet:
Computer vision techniques, together with image surveys, can reconstruct 3D shapes of the photographed objects, providing geometric information relevant to the structural conditions. Some researchers have investigated approaches for converting the reconstructed shapes into structural mesh models directly, e.g., (Zhang & Lin, 2021). While such purely data driven approaches demonstrate promising results, their integration into existing digital twin frameworks is not necessarily straightforward. One of the reasons is that FE models used by typical digital twin applications put modeling assumptions and simplifications, e.g., using beam models, not 3D solid models that replicate the target structural geometry exactly. Those modeling assumptions are the consequence of engineering decisions related to the purpose of the model and the expected levels of detail. An approach to updating digital twin models systematically in a manner consistent with those modeling assumptions is a key to integrating 3D geometric measurement into existing digital twin frameworks. 

A framework for incorporating computer vision-based 3D reconstruction and geometry measurement into digital twin models for structural dynamics applications has been proposed by the author's group, which is shown in Figure 2 ( Lai et al., 2022). Starting from a simplified initial FE model (beam elements are considered therein), the framework performs a sequence of vibration measurement and image surveys to update model material and geometric properties, respectively. The vibration-based model updating is performed by the measurement by accelerometers and/or computer vision techniques, followed by the application of Bayesian model updating techniques, e.g., (Yuen et al., 2006). The geometry update is performed in the following steps: (1) image survey and 3D reconstruction by Structure from Motion (SfM) method, (2) alignment of digital twin model to the reconstructed mesh Figure 2 Framework for digital twin model updating based on vibration measurement and computer vision-based 3D reconstruction (Lai et al., 2022). 

model, (3) slicing the reconstructed mesh model along the aligned beam elements of the digital twin model, (4) evaluating and updating cross-sectional geometric properties, such as areas and second moments of area. This research demonstrates the use of the same simple structural model consistently for different types of model updating, showing promising preliminary results for the detection and quantification of damage in the context of long-term structural health monitoring.

documents.title: Post-Earthquake Building Evaluation Using UAVs: A BIM-Based Digital Twin Framework
documents.snippet:
Such approaches typically generate a 3D reconstruction from site photographs aligned in the BIM geometric reference frame. Once aligned, semantic information stored in the BIM is used to track construction progress. For example, the user can assess, on an element-wise basis, whether construction is on schedule and whether the as-built geometry conforms to the design. BIM can fill a similar role for post-earthquake inspection, providing a way to store data, establish a geometric reference frame for UAV imagery, and efficiently organize and classify structural components by overlaying BIM on photographs. Using BIM requires either a modern target building, where a BIM is created as part of the design process, or sufficient stakeholder investment to justify creating a BIM to aid in post-earthquake inspection. On its own, however, BIM is not predictive; to predict global damage and future performance, the BIM and visual survey must be combined with an analytical model of the building. 

Digital twins have been proposed as a means to provide predictive information about an as-built structure. As used herein, a digital twin is a physics-based probabilistic simulation model that is continuously updated using sensor information and load history from the physical system [30]. Such systems have been proposed and deployed for manufacturing, industrial, aerospace, and civil engineering applications [31,32]. In civil structural health monitoring, frameworks have been proposed that meet the criteria of a digital twin. For example, Hughes et al. [33] described a probabilistic system for risk assessment and decision making using sensor data and demonstrate its application on a laboratory truss structure. Zhu et al. [34] developed a real-time digital twin framework for structural health monitoring applications using vibration data, whereby the digital model can be continuously and efficiently updated to reflect changes to the structure. Gardner et al. [35] proposed a scheme to characterize and predict unanticipated nonlinear acceleration responses with a digital twin. However, while useful for updating a digital twin for predicting seismic response, many of these examples have been limited to simulation or scaled laboratory experiments. Angjeliu et al. [36] developed a digital twin model of a historic cathedral in Milan, Italy, and successfully predict existing damage using their calibrated digital twin to model the evolution of the structure through its lifetime.

# Short Answer

- Structural health monitoring (SHM) implementations yield conflicting digital twin (DT) prediction accuracy primarily because system architectures, sensor/signal choices, and data–model integration are case-specific and often under-specified; uncertainties from measurements, environmental/operational variability (EOV), modeling errors, and ill-posed inverse problems propagate into updates, while inconsistent synchronization and data quality further degrade outcomes. <cite id="63cd575a-1">There is no consensus on digital twin architectures or internal elements in civil engineering, which hinders operability and reliability of DT-based SHM; a generic reference architecture is needed to enhance performance</cite> <cite id="63cd575a-3">Field DT implementations depend strongly on case-specific sensor types/locations, model development, and data fusion algorithms; this variability drives implementation-dependent performance</cite> <cite id="35f20942-0">Deterministic FE updating accuracy and spatial resolution depend on data accuracy/completeness and model fidelity, with uncertainties from measurement noise, estimation errors, and changing environmental conditions propagating into the updating process; modeling errors further add uncertainty, necessitating probabilistic frameworks</cite> <cite id="45b21912-2">DTs often assume deterministic sensing and simulation, but pervasive uncertainties arise from measurement, modeling, and operational variability (e.g., temperature/humidity effects on stress sensors); these can compromise accuracy</cite> <cite id="45b21912-0">Continuous synchronization and metadata/data management are major practical challenges when combining heterogeneous datasets for DT updating</cite>.

- Finite element model updating improves DT outcomes when the SHM system is designed for identifiability (adequate excitation and sensor coverage), the updating and uncertainty quantification (UQ) pipeline is robust (e.g., Bayesian/probabilistic with regularization), initial models are reasonably accurate, and quantities of interest (KPIs) are well-linked between model and measurements; improvements are most reliable for global diagnostics and unmeasured locations, and when indirect updating via sensors is carefully designed and validated. <cite id="35f20942-3">As-built FEMs often deviate from real structures due to construction tolerances and material property degradation; updating is necessary to bring model predictions closer to reality</cite> <cite id="35f20942-0">Probabilistic (Bayesian) updating quantifies parameter uncertainty by integrating prior knowledge with measured data, addressing uncertainties from measurements and modeling</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-1">Vibration-based SHM/FE updating faces ill-posed and ill-conditioned inverse problems due to noise, modeling errors, and data scarcity; Bayesian updating provides a rigorous probabilistic framework with quantified uncertainty</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-3">Stochastic model updating yields multiple posterior solutions that reveal global/local identifiability or unidentifiability, quantify parameter uncertainties, and propagate them to responses for risk assessment</cite> <cite id="45b21912-0">Once updated, DTs can predict KPIs (e.g., stresses at unmeasured locations, remaining useful life), enabling diagnostics and prognostics beyond local sensor coverage</cite> <cite id="45b21912-3">Direct parameter updating via in situ tests is most accurate but costly and limited in frequency/coverage; indirect sensor-based updating is easier but can introduce higher uncertainty if monitoring and updating procedures are poorly designed</cite>.

# Why SHM Implementations Yield Conflicting DT Prediction Accuracy

SHM-based digital twins differ across applications in modeling assumptions, sensor networks, feature extraction, and decision pipelines; without aligned architectures and data standards, commensurate accuracy is hard to achieve. <cite id="63cd575a-1">The lack of consensus on DT definitions and architectures leads to heterogeneous implementations whose performance varies without a shared basis</cite> <cite id="63cd575a-3">DT effectiveness hinges on sensor types/locations, model development, and data fusion tailored to objectives; this case-specificity produces divergent outcomes even for similar structures</cite> <cite id="45b21912-4">Practical marine-structure DTs require model updating, real-time simulation, and data-driven forecasting, yet challenges include long-term monitored data quality, standardization, and redundancy</cite>.

Data-driven inputs to the DT are themselves uncertain and time-varying. <cite id="35f20942-0">Uncertainties from measurement noise, estimation errors, and environmental changes propagate through updating and reduce accuracy of deterministic solutions; modeling errors from idealizations add further error</cite> <cite id="45b21912-2">Operational uncertainties—variability under different conditions and human interactions—can cause deterministic DTs to deviate markedly (e.g., temperature/humidity-dependent sensor biases), degrading predictive accuracy</cite>. These uncertainties are often asymmetrically distributed across structural scales and modes; if only localized or modal features are used without global linkage, predictions outside measured regions remain unreliable. <cite id="63cd575a-4">DTs enable all-over monitoring and virtual sensing at unmonitored locations, improving diagnostics and prognostics compared to conventional SHM that samples only selected locations</cite>.

Model fidelity and pipeline integration also create cross-case inconsistencies. <cite id="35f20942-1">Predictive accuracy is inherently tied to the fidelity of the as-built finite element model; integrating UQ and damage-informed inputs is needed for real-world SHM applicability</cite> <cite id="45b21912-0">Continuous DT updating requires robust data management (real-time access, preprocessing, synchronization, and metadata schemas), where synchronization challenges arise especially when fusing heterogeneous datasets</cite>. When synchronization, filtering, and feature alignment are weak, the same physics-based model can show large accuracy swings between deployments. <cite id="63cd575a-3">Implementation challenges include sensor noise and data fusion algorithm choices that strongly influence performance</cite>.

# What Determines When FEM Updating Improves Outcomes

Improvements depend on whether the inverse problem is observable and solvable with the available data, and on robustness of the updating/UQ pipeline.

- Measured information must be informative about the parameters of interest. <cite id="35f20942-0">Accuracy and spatial resolution of deterministic damage identification depend on the accuracy and completeness of measured data or extracted features; uncertainties in these features propagate into updating results</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-1">Noise, modeling errors, and data scarcity lead to ill-posed/ill-conditioned inverse problems; Bayesian updating integrates prior knowledge with data to quantify uncertainty and stabilize solutions</cite>. Practical strategies exist to make such problems well-posed: <cite id="298d94cd-4">Regularization and hybrid iterative methods within sensitivity-based FEMU can address ill-posedness under incomplete noisy modal data, improving accuracy on benchmark frames and trusses</cite>.

- The SHM hardware and sampling must excite and observe the modes/fields driving the KPIs. <cite id="35f20942-3">Bridges and other structures drift from design parameters; accurate initial FEMs are essential for damage detection, motivating updating when measured responses deviate</cite> <cite id="45b21912-3">If great care is not taken in designing the monitoring system and updating procedures, indirect (sensor-based) updating may lead to a higher degree of uncertainty than direct parameter updating</cite>. Excitation content (e.g., ambient vs. forced vibration) and sensor placement determine which modes are identifiable; insufficient spatial coverage and low-frequency excitation limit localization/severity estimates and can leave hidden damage unidentifiable. <cite id="298d94cd-1">Modal-acceleration methods exhibit limitations when data lack sufficient content or coverage, underscoring the need for observability-aware design</cite>.

- Initial model fidelity and update scope/strategy matter. <cite id="35f20942-3">Deviation from actual structures (material property changes, geometric deterioration) necessitates updating to reduce discrepancies in predictions</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-3">Determining global vs. local identifiability and quantifying posterior uncertainties via multiple solutions helps avoid overconfident misupdates and informs when propagation to KPIs will be reliable</cite>.

- Uncertainty propagation to KPIs must be controlled. <cite id="35f20942-0">Probabilistic updating quantifies posterior parameter distributions and their uncertainties, improving the accuracy of model-predicted quantities</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-3">Posterior analysis reveals invariant parameter regions and quantifies how parameter uncertainty propagates into modal properties and structural responses, enabling risk assessment</cite>. If UQ is absent or crude, reported “improvements” may mask hidden uncertainty, yielding inconsistent gains across KPIs and time.

- Decision and data integration pipelines must align with objectives. <cite id="45b21912-0">A DT closes the loop from measurements to model updates to predictions (KPIs such as stress, deformation, or remaining useful life) and then to adaptive decisions; this cyclic integration improves diagnostics/prognostics when implemented robustly</cite> <cite id="45b21912-3">When monitoring starts years after operation, the DT often reduces to a calibrated design-stage model that matches measured responses, limiting predictive power unless additional direct measurements or targeted inspections refine parameters</cite> <cite id="45b21912-4">Standardization, redundancy, and data quality assurance are key to exploiting DT potential over long horizons</cite>.

# When Improvements Fail or Are Misleading

- Insufficient or noisy excitation and sparse/erratic sensors reduce identifiability and inflate uncertainty. <cite id="298d94cd-1">Noise and data scarcity cause ill-posed inverse problems; without Bayesian integration and regularization, parameter estimates become unreliable</cite> <cite id="35f20942-0">Uncertainties from estimation errors and changing environmental conditions propagate to uncertain updates</cite>.

- Environmental/operational variability (EOV) is not modeled or synchronized. <cite id="45b21912-2">Measurement biases tied to temperature/humidity can shift sensor readouts significantly, compromising deterministic DT accuracy</cite>. When EOV is ignored or inconsistently handled, apparent accuracy gains are fragile and may reverse under changing conditions.

- Overfitting to transient conditions or noise, and lack of cross-validation. <cite id="35f20942-0">Deterministic updates can achieve good fit to noisy/uncertain features but yield uncertain spatial resolution and overfit to measurement artifacts</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-3">Single-peaked posteriors can be locally optimal yet miss global structure; multiple-solution analyses expose flat regions and unidentifiable parameter sets, preventing reliable KPI prediction</cite>.

- Pipeline integration gaps defeat benefits. <cite id="45b21912-0">Synchronization and metadata challenges arise when fusing heterogeneous datasets; poor real-time access and preprocessing degrade updates</cite> <cite id="63cd575a-3">Case-specific dependencies on sensor types/locations and fusion algorithms lead to variability and missed opportunities for all-over monitoring</cite>.

- Monitoring too late or with limited direct access. <cite id="45b21912-3">If monitoring starts years after construction, indirect updating can only match measured responses at accessible locations; the DT emulates design-stage parameters and lacks deeper identifiability</cite>.

# Practical Guidance: Designing for Reliable Improvement

1) Choose measurable, identifiable KPIs and link them to model degrees of freedom. <cite id="45b21912-0">Define KPIs (e.g., stresses at unmeasured locations, remaining life) and ensure the DT’s predictive loop explicitly targets these quantities</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-1">Use modal properties from accelerometers but recognize limitations of acceleration-based methods when content/coverage are inadequate</cite>.

2) Engineer observability: excitation and sensor placement. <cite id="298d94cd-1">Ensure modal content and spatial coverage necessary for the targeted parameters; ill-posedness and ill-conditioning otherwise hinder accurate updating</cite> <cite id="298d94cd-4">Adopt sensitivity-based frameworks with regularization (e.g., hybrid iterative methods) to stabilize updates under incomplete noisy data</cite>.
